title: Fatalities are rare events
article: Unlike their counterparts in shoot'em up movies and television cop shows, most police officers go their entire careers without shooting, let alone killing, someone in the line of duty.

Those who do must come to terms with their own vulnerability and, depending on the circumstances of the shooting, their remorse. They must also endure harsh questioning as investigators deconstruct, over weeks and sometimes months, an incident that transpired in a heartbeat.
"Police officers are sworn to protect life and liberty and the taking of someone's life is tragic and very difficult for the person (who) has to do it," said Windsor Police Staff Sgt. Neal Jessop.
"You react according to your training and your conscience. In a moment it's over."
In a career spanning more than 30 years, Jessop has fired his revolver but never trained its sights on someone and pulled the trigger.
"I've fired in a warning situation and to draw attention to myself," he said.
"In 31 years, I've never shot at anyone. I'm extremely thankful for that."
Windsor Police Staff Sgt. Ed McNorton has taken his revolver out of his holster several times during his 28 years on the job but has never used deadly force.
"It's not anything that any one of us ever wants to confront. It's a worst case scenario," he said.
Including Monday's fatal shooting of Robert Scott Carpenter by an unidentified Amherstburg police officer, at least five civilians have been shot and killed by Ontario police officers this year.
Dr. David Hoath, a staff psychologist with the OPP, said police officers who shoot and kill someone in the line of duty face an uphill battle but generally continue with careers in policing.
"It certainly is stressful and it can be life-disrupting," he said, adding officers have an elaborate support network including professional psychologists and trained, peer counsellors.
Hoath said the officer must confront a violated sense of security if they were placed in a life-threatening situation and deal with the fact they killed.
And they must do that in the face of intense media scrutiny. "The investigation is a complicating factor."
